subcategory: pine rockland and tropical hammock native tree

planting.note: Transplant container-grown trees in spring into thin, rocky limestone or sandy soil, choosing a site with full sun to light shade since this slow grower resents being moved once its deep root system takes hold.

directions: Black ironwood is a dense, slow-growing evergreen of south Florida pine rocklands and hardwood hammocks, prized for wood so hard and heavy it barely floats, and for glossy, leathery leaves that hold up through drought and salt-laden wind. Set container stock into sharply drained limestone or sandy soil in spring, watering regularly only through the first year while the taproot establishes. Small greenish flowers appear most of the year and are followed by shiny black drupes that songbirds and small mammals seek out through fall and winter. Once established it needs no fertilizer and tolerates extended dry spells, making it a durable specimen or clipped screen for rockland-style native gardens.

subcategory: pine rockland and tropical hammock native tree

planting.note: Transplant container stock in spring into well-drained limestone or sandy soil in full sun to light shade, watering consistently the first season to establish the slow-forming root system.

directions: Torchwood is a small, aromatic hammock and pineland tree whose resin-rich wood was historically split and burned as makeshift torches, a trait that also makes crushed leaves pleasantly citrusy when bruised. Plant container specimens in spring in well-drained, limestone-influenced or sandy soil, siting them in full sun to light shade along a hammock edge or pineland-style border. Clusters of small white flowers appear nearly year-round and peak in spring, followed by small black fruit that birds favor, and the foliage serves as a larval host for giant swallowtail and other native butterflies. Keep soil evenly moist through the first year; established plants handle brief drought but do best without prolonged dry spells.

planting.note: Transplant container-grown trees in spring into humus-topped limestone or sandy soil beneath an open canopy, since this rare hammock species establishes best with some high shade while young.

directions: Redberry stopper is a very slow-growing tropical hammock understory tree with a narrow, upright crown of thick, glossy, dark green leaves that each taper to a distinct drip tip. Plant container stock in spring in moist, well-drained limestone or sandy soil with a humus-rich top layer, siting it in dappled shade beneath taller canopy trees or in a partly shaded hammock-style bed. Clusters of small white flowers open intermittently through the year, heaviest in spring and summer, and ripen into red berries that attract fruit-eating birds. Because the species is state-listed as endangered in the wild, garden plantings grown from nursery stock contribute meaningfully to its conservation while asking little beyond steady moisture during establishment.

subcategory: tropical hammock understory to canopy tree

planting.note: Transplant container-grown trees in spring into well-drained hammock soil in partial shade while young, since seedlings establish best under an existing canopy before growing on toward full sun.

directions: Inkwood is a dense-canopied tropical hammock tree named for the dark juice of its small black fruit, once used informally as a makeshift ink; the glossy compound leaves give year-round cover for nesting and roosting birds. Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, limestone-based or sandy soil, giving young trees partial shade before they mature into a fuller-sun canopy position. Fragrant small white flowers cluster along the branches from late winter into summer and draw a range of pollinating insects. Once rooted, inkwood tolerates drought and occasional salt spray, needing only light pruning to shape a strong, long-lived shade tree.

planting.note: Transplant container stock in spring into well-drained limestone or sandy soil in dappled shade, since this understory Myrtaceae shrub colors and fills in best out of harsh midday sun.

directions: Spicewood is a small, aromatic hammock understory shrub in the myrtle family, its new growth flushing pink to red before settling into glossy, light green leaves that release a spicy scent when crushed. Plant container specimens in spring in well-drained, limestone-influenced soil, siting them in partial shade beneath hammock canopy where the species naturally grows as a sub-canopy layer. Mildly fragrant, inconspicuous white to beige flowers open in spring and summer, and the distinctive lidded flower buds characteristic of the genus give way to red-to-black berries by fall that songbirds readily take. Because the species is state-listed as threatened, nursery-propagated plants in shaded native beds help take pressure off remaining wild populations.

planting.note: Transplant container-grown trees in spring into well-drained sandy or limestone soil in full sun to partial sun; lancewood grows quickly once rooted and needs no special soil amendment.

directions: Lancewood is a fast-growing hammock tree named for its narrow, lance-shaped, aromatic leaves, forming a dense, slender-branched canopy that works well as a screen, buffer, or small shade tree in south and central Florida hammock-style landscapes. Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, sandy or limestone soil in full sun to partial sun, watering regularly only through the first season. Clusters of small, fragrant white flowers open from late winter into spring and attract a variety of pollinating insects, while the foliage serves as a larval host for several native swallowtail butterflies. Highly drought tolerant once established, it also handles moderate salt exposure, making it a versatile choice near the coast.

planting.note: Transplant container-grown trees in spring into well-drained sandy or limestone soil in full sun, giving regular water the first year while the root system establishes.

directions: Willow bustic takes its common name from narrow, willow-like leaves borne on a tall, straight-trunked hammock canopy tree valued as an accent or shade specimen in south Florida native landscapes. Plant container stock in spring in full sun on well-drained sandy or limestone soil, watering consistently through the establishment year before easing off. Small, fragrant white flowers cluster along the branches and ripen into black fruit that draws fruit-eating birds through the cooler months. Growth is steady rather than fast, and mature trees tolerate drought well but perform best away from heavy salt exposure.

subcategory: pine rockland and coastal hammock native shrub

planting.note: Transplant container-grown shrubs in spring into well-drained sandy or limestone soil in full sun to part shade; this multi-trunked shrub tolerates poor, rocky ground once its roots take hold.

directions: Keys blackbead is a dense, multi-trunked shrub of rockland and coastal hammock edges, its puffball clusters of white to pale pink flowers opening from winter into spring on a broad, irregular, leathery-leaved crown. Set container plants in spring into sharply drained sandy or limestone soil in full sun to part shade, watering regularly only until established. Spiraling green seedpods dry and split by summer to reveal bright red arils around black seeds, a display that draws seed-eating birds and makes the plant a reliable larval host for cassius blue and large orange sulphur butterflies. Once rooted it shrugs off drought and poor soil, needing only occasional thinning to maintain an open, wind-firm form.
